reception.text: Opponents seized on the monument's size, and Ralph Cameron, who held mining claims at the head of the Bright Angel Trail, refused to yield.

political_impact.text: Cameron kept collecting a one-dollar toll on the Bright Angel Trail until Coconino County took it over in 1912.
Senate bills to make the canyon a national park were introduced again in 1910 and 1911, with the monument in place, and died.

legacy.text: The monument held the line for eleven years until Congress made the canyon a national park in 1919, the outcome Roosevelt had wanted.

Ruling against Cameron, a unanimous Supreme Court held that the Grand Canyon is an object of scientific interest under the Antiquities Act; it did not address the Act's smallest-area limit, though later courts cite the case for broad presidential discretion.
As senator from 1921, Cameron fought the National Park Service and cut the park's appropriation from $100,000 for fiscal 1922 to $75,000 for fiscal 1923.
Cameron lost his Senate seat to Carl Hayden in November 1926, 44,591 to 31,845, after a Los Angeles Times series alleged he had salted mining claims in the canyon.
The designation remains the classic example of the Antiquities Act used boldly, a line running to the 2023 Baaj Nwaavjo I'tah Kukveni-Ancestral Footprints of the Grand Canyon National Monument.

today.name: Grand Canyon National Park
today.note: The 1919 act revoked the monument and folded its lands into the park; 4,919,163 recreation visits in 2024.
today.source: Act of February 26, 1919, 40 Stat. 1175; NPS Grand Canyon Park Profile (2025)

related.note: Roosevelt's 1906 game preserve on the Kaibab Plateau, north and west of the Colorado River, in the same forest reserve.
Devils Tower, the first Antiquities Act monument, first read the law to cover natural wonders.

later_actions.text: Congress created Grand Canyon National Park, revoking the monument and folding its lands into the park.
The Supreme Court ruled against Ralph Cameron's Cape Horn mining claim and rejected his argument that the monument lacked authority.
Congress cut the park's appropriation to $75,000 for fiscal 1923, from $100,000 the year before.

uncertain: Cameron's February 1922 Senate speech is known only from a New York Times search excerpt; only the phrase "thirty or forty millionaires" is confirmed.
